children: Wells Fargo Securities on Wednesday downgraded three construction materials companies and upgraded Martin Marietta Materials
as analyst Timna Tanners warned that weaker government spending, elevated interest rates and soft housing demand could pressure industry volumes in 2027.
Tanners lowered Amrize
and Eagle Materials
to Equal Weight from Overweight. She cut Vulcan Materials to Underweight from Equal Weight, while raising Martin Marietta
to Overweight from Equal Weight and naming it her top pick in the group.

The ratings changes reflect a widening divide between companies that may benefit from acquisitions and those more exposed to slowing construction markets. Wells Fargo now expects organic industry volumes to fall about 5% next year, leaving most of its 2027 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization forecasts below Wall Street estimates.
Martin Marietta’s price target rose to $609 from $581. Price targets fell to $44 from $55 for Amrize, $196 from $231 for Eagle Materials and $254 from $305 for Vulcan.
Wells Fargo maintained its Overweight rating on CRH
but cut its price target to $107 from $132. Knife River
remained Equal Weight, with its target reduced to $62 from $73.
Martin Marietta becomes top pick
Martin Marietta’s
recent acquisitions distinguish it from peers facing a difficult demand environment, according to the report.

The company completed its $13.5 billion acquisition of Lhoist North America in August. Wells Fargo expects the lime business to strengthen margins over time as Martin Marietta passes through higher costs in a more consolidated market.

Tanners also sees room for pricing improvements at assets acquired through the company’s New Frontier Materials purchase and its quarry exchange with Quikrete. Those operations currently have prices below Martin Marietta’s legacy portfolio.

Wells Fargo forecasts Martin Marietta will generate $3.25 billion in EBITDA during 2027, about 16% above the current FactSet consensus. Tanners said analysts’ estimates may not yet fully reflect the Lhoist transaction.
The firm expects third-quarter EBITDA of $843 million, compared with the consensus estimate of $779 million.
Vulcan cut on infrastructure risks
Wells Fargo downgraded Vulcan Materials
after the stock outperformed its peers this year, leaving its valuation harder to justify amid deteriorating construction trends.

Highways account for about 20% of Vulcan’s aggregates demand, exposing the company to uncertainty surrounding federal infrastructure funding and constrained state budgets. Wells Fargo also expects weak residential and nonresidential construction, with relatively little benefit from data-center development.
The firm cut its 2027 ebitda estimate for Vulcan
to $2.42 billion from $2.74 billion, putting the forecast about 11% below consensus. The estimate assumes aggregates volumes decline 5%, partly offset by a 3.6% increase in pricing.
Vulcan shares closed Tuesday at $258.30, slightly above Wells Fargo’s new $254 target.
Amrize faces execution concerns
Amrize’s
downgrade reflects both the weaker demand forecast and company-specific execution concerns following several disappointing results.

Wells Fargo pointed to subdued cement pricing, softer demand for building-envelope products and turnover in several finance and investor-relations positions. The changes come as Amrize continues establishing its independent reporting and control systems following its separation from Holcim.
Tanners cut her 2027 EBITDA forecast by 15% to $2.92 billion, also about 15% below consensus. She expects weaker margins in both the Building Materials and Building Envelope divisions.
Amrize shares closed Tuesday at $41.95, leaving limited upside to the new $44 price target.
Eagle Materials lacks near-term catalysts
Eagle Materials
retains some of the sector’s strongest EBITDA margins and free cash flow characteristics, but Wells Fargo believes those advantages are largely reflected in the stock’s valuation.

Higher interest rates are expected to continue pressuring housing and other construction markets. Data centers offer some incremental cement demand, but Wells Fargo estimates they could represent only about 2.5% to 3% of total U.S. cement consumption by 2030.
The firm lowered its fiscal 2028 ebitda estimate for Eagle Materials
by 7% to $740 million. Its new $196 price target offers little upside from Tuesday’s closing price of $190.58.
Highway funding clouds industry outlook

The cautious industry view centers partly on uncertainty over federal road spending. A recently enacted continuing resolution left about $9.5 billion in annualized highway and bridge funding outside the extended authorization, according to the report.

That represents roughly 13% of fiscal 2026 federal highway investment. After accounting for construction-cost inflation, Wells Fargo estimates federal highway purchasing power could fall about 17% in 2027.

An initial House proposal to replace the 2021 infrastructure law also calls for only about 0.2% growth in first-year highway funding. That would amount to a decline in real construction activity if costs continue rising near their current pace.

Higher diesel and other energy costs pose an additional threat to margins. Some producers protected 2026 profitability by buying asphalt supplies before energy prices increased, but those benefits may fade next year.
Wells Fargo remains positive on CRH
because of its acquisition strategy, asset sales and history of execution. Even so, the firm lowered its 2027 ebitda estimate for the company to $7.9 billion, about 12% below consensus.

Across the group, Tanners said enthusiasm for data-center construction cannot compensate for weakness in housing, highways and traditional nonresidential projects. Data centers still represent less than 5% of overall construction-materials demand, leaving the industry closely tied to interest rates and public spending.

title: Wells Fargo shuffles building materials ratings as 2027 outlook weakens
